guide.text:
Bellingham Math Circle / Week 35 / Adult facilitator guide
Footprint borders facilitator guide
Mathematical overview
Object. A border is the ideal infinite repetition in both directions of a finite motif arrangement,
bounded across the strip. Only footprints and their orientations count. Ends, guide lines and
temporary labels do not. The intended examples are discrete, nonempty patterns with a shortest
positive translation P along the border. Finite scraps alone do not establish an infinite symmetry.
Glide theorem. Write H(x,y) = (x,-y) for reflection in the middle line and T_a(x,y) = (x+a,y) for a
slide along it. They commute. A glide G_a = T_a H with a ≠ 0 satisfies G_a² = T_2a. Thus a
matching 3 cm glide forces a matching 6 cm slide, but need not force a 3 cm slide or the bare
reflection H.
Shortest distances. If a border has a glide along this line but H itself fails, its shortest glide
length is P/2. Every glide displacement is (k + 1/2)P, k an integer. If H is a symmetry instead,
matching glide displacements are kP; the shortest nonzero glide length is P. These statements
require a primitive translation P and a fixed glide axis; an arbitrary matching glide need not be the
shortest.
Forced motions. Reflections in two perpendicular lines compose to a half-turn about their
crossing. The printed crossing lines are perpendicular. For general crossing lines the rotation angle
is twice their angle; a half-turn is not a theorem for arbitrary crossing lines. Every composition or
inverse of symmetries is a symmetry.
Limits. There are seven discrete frieze symmetry types, but these problems do not prove or
require that classification. A simple motif can accidentally add symmetries. The specified notched
F-like motif has no nonidentity planar isometry, so its handedness and direction distinguish
candidate moves.
What children are meant to discover
• K-1: Build repeating borders and use a copy to distinguish slides, flips, glides and half-turns. A
local matching attempt is evidence to investigate the repeated rule.
• Grades 2-3: Find a glide that works although the flip alone fails; compare shortest distances
and change which motions a border permits.
• Grades 4-5: Explain forced symmetries by composition and justify a full symmetry description
for one chosen construction. Sampling several moves is not a proof of completeness.
Status. The current K-1 packet has seven problems on five pages; the two older v2 packets retain
six problems each. Mathematical examples are verified; physical cutout handling and classroom
pacing are untested. The Grades 2-3 edit explicitly permits moved footprints and a larger
repeating part.
Unpiloted / Current base packets / Revised October 4 2026 1

Bellingham Math Circle / Week 35 / Adult facilitator guide
Preparation and session plan
Materials and readiness
For eleven children, use three adult-led tables. Three-child groups can rotate builder, tester and
observer; budget five pair-sized material sets overall. Per pair supply 20-24 reusable footprint
pieces, four paper strips at least 70 by 280 mm, two tracing strips, a pencil or washable marker,
and a ruler. Provide a 600 mm joined demonstration strip per table. Keep repeated motifs
separated and use at least three or four visible repeats.
Motifs: use the exact notched F-like outline printed in the introduction, at least 25 mm long, with
its direction arrow. Supply the original, its horizontal mirror, its vertical mirror and its half-turn;
ordinary symmetric footprints can change the answers. An economical alternative is identical
rectangular cards carrying those drawings. State that card edges and blank backgrounds are
handling aids, not pattern data. Prepare visible marks on both sides or use tracing paper so a
reflection can be enacted accurately. Adults cut and prepare pieces, not children during the
investigation.
Preparation estimate: 30-45 minutes for a first reusable set, substantially less when reusing it.
Before class, check that the chosen pieces really distinguish all four forms, test one reflected
tracing strip, and rehearse the common launch. The packet is not a complete manipulative kit. If
the exact outline is hard to reproduce, trace and copy its printed example rather than substitute a
symmetric stamp without checking it.
Readiness: children need to extend a repeating arrangement and compare a moved copy with
every motif in the original. Reading and measured lengths can be adult-supported; the youngest
can compare slide lengths directly. If keeping the original fixed or mentally continuing the ends is
difficult, spend the session on one border and slide matching.
Common launch
Let children handle pieces first. Start K-1 with one repeating row and a tracing copy: slide the copy
to a matching position and a position that fails. Keep the original fixed. Introduce the single-motif
flip-then-slide visual only before the first glide task. Keep the label A with the same piece during
the demonstration. This teaches the move without giving a target border. Compare two or three
interior repetitions; explain that the printed ends are a window on an endless pattern.
Demonstrate a half-turn about a chosen point when first needed, including a point between
motifs.
Flexible hour
0-8 minutes: handling and launch. 8-23: two different shortest periods, then the glide challenge.
Let a successful pattern remain on one strip while a second is built. 23-27: movement break,
using a hand-held copy to show a slide and a half-turn. 27-45: selected reflection/half-turn
construction or edit. 45-56: partner testing and one explanation of a forced motion. 56-60: save
the generating rule and note what children could actually justify.
A good stopping point is one border with a well-defended unusual symmetry. Upper Problem 6 can
occupy an entire later discussion. Offer hints only when needed: “Where must this one footprint
land?” then “Does its direction agree?” then “What happens if you do your matching move twice?”

Bellingham Math Circle / Week 35 / Adult facilitator guide
Concrete answer bank
A precise way to read these examples
Let the middle line be y = 0. Let A be the printed asymmetric footprint, H A its reflection across a
horizontal line, V A its reflection across a vertical line, and R A its half-turn. These names describe
the entire footprint, including its direction arrow. Positions below are motif anchors in centimeters;
translate the same anchor consistently. Take h = 1.5 cm and use the original motif at about 26
mm wide. In every recipe, k is any integer, so the pattern continues both ways.
Border T, slides only: put A at (6k, h). The primitive period is 6 cm. A variant with A at (4k, h)
has primitive period 4 cm. A translation must take an A anchor to another A anchor, so no smaller
positive slide works. A half-turn would reverse the asymmetric motif; no reversed motif is present.
Border G, a glide without its bare reflection: put A at (6k, h) and H A at (6k + 3, -h). A 3 cm
rightward glide takes an upper A to the next lower H A and that lower piece to the next upper A.
The shortest glide is 3 cm and the shortest slide is 6 cm. A bare horizontal flip lands in the gaps. A
3 cm bare slide lands on the wrong row. No vertical reflection or half-turn matches because it
would introduce V A or R A, neither of which occurs.
Border H, a horizontal reflection without any half-turn: put A at (6k, h) and H A at (6k, -h).
The middle-line flip matches paired motifs. Every half-turn changes the direction/handedness to R
A or V A, forms absent from the border. Horizontal glides by nonzero multiples of 6 cm also work.
Border R, half-turns without reflections: put A at (6k, h) and R A at (6k + 3, -h). Half-turn
about (1.5, 0) matches, and so do half-turns about (1.5 + 3k, 0). The shortest slide is 6 cm.
Horizontal or vertical reflection introduces H A or V A, so neither type of reflection matches. No
glide works either.
Border E, both perpendicular reflections: repeat four motifs every 6 cm: A at (1.5, h), V A at
(-1.5, h), H A at (1.5, -h), and R A at (-1.5, -h). Reflection in y = 0 and in x = 0 both match. Their
composition is the half-turn about (0,0). The primitive slide is 6 cm; a 3 cm slide preserves
locations but changes the required motif orientations.
Checking a child's own border
These are witnesses, not the only solutions. Ask for the repeating part and test its seams as well
as its interior. A drawing with three locally similar motifs may fail at a join. A complete argument
uses a generating rule and shows where every kind of motif lands. When excluding a motion, a
single unavoidable mismatch is enough. Do not infer the shortest period from the length of the
block the child happened to draw.

Bellingham Math Circle / Week 35 / Adult facilitator guide
Keys for K-1 and Grades 2-3
K-1 continuation, Problems 2-7
Problem 2: Border T with 4 cm spacing and with 6 cm spacing gives two different shortest slides.
The child need not name centimeters; compare the moved copies. Repeating a 4 cm block twice
does not make an 8 cm primitive period.
Problem 3: Border G is a witness: a flip and 3 cm slide works; the flip alone fails. It is enough for a
child to demonstrate those two facts on several repeats and describe the continuation.
Problem 4: Another G border with top motifs at 8k and bottom mirrored motifs at 8k + 4 has the
same kind of match but a different size. Alternatively change the motif's vertical distance from the
middle line while keeping the paired offsets consistent. Preserve the nonzero parallel slide
requirement.
Problem 5: Start with Border H. Shift every lower-row mirrored footprint 3 cm right to obtain
Border G; the old middle-line reflection now fails. Repeat the same edit in every 6 cm block so the
new border still repeats.
Problem 6: Border R matches after a half-turn about (1.5,0). Border T has no matching half-turn
about any point, because no half-turned footprint occurs anywhere. Testing just a printed tick as a
center is not sufficient.
Problem 7: Answers depend on the traded borders. Use the recipes on page 3 as checks, not as a
required catalog. Encourage the tester to show a matching move and a failed move, with the
whole repeat accounted for.
Grades 2-3
Problem 1: Border T at 4 cm and 6 cm spacings. Mark the displacement of a particular motif on
the tracing copy. Its image must be the nearest next A for the shortest positive match.
Problem 2: Border G. Neither the bare horizontal flip nor the 3 cm bare slide works, although
their glide does.
Problem 3: On every border satisfying Problem 2, the shortest glide is half the shortest slide. In G
these are 3 and 6 cm. This is a theorem under the stated discrete-period assumptions, not just a
feature of the example; proof on page 6.
Problem 4: Border H has the requested flip and no half-turn about any point. The asymmetric
motif rules out the reversed orientations a half-turn would need.
Problem 5: Border R works. Its middle-line flip fails. The task does not demand the absence of all
other reflections, but this witness has none.
Problem 6: One simple edit is H to G above, breaking the old reflection and keeping period 6. To
break an old translation instead, start with T at x = 6k. In every 12 cm block move the footprint at
x = 12k to x = 12k + 0.5, leaving the one at x = 12k + 6 unchanged. The new gaps alternate 5.5
and 6.5 cm. The old 6 cm slide fails and a 12 cm slide works. This edit uses the explicitly allowed
larger repeating part; it is not a one-off defect in an otherwise endless unchanged border.

Bellingham Math Circle / Week 35 / Adult facilitator guide
Key for Grades 4-5
Problem 1: Border T with periods 4 and 6 cm. Since each motif is asymmetric, a matching
translation preserves its form and takes an anchor to an anchor. Consecutive anchors are
precisely 4 or 6 cm apart, excluding smaller positive translations. An unnecessarily large chosen
repeat is not evidence of a large primitive period.
Problem 2: Border G has shortest slide 6 cm and shortest glide 3 cm. Tracking one upper A forces
slide displacement into 6 times an integer, or glide displacement into 3 plus 6 times an integer.
Each permitted displacement also maps the lower mirrored row correctly.
Problem 3: A 6 cm slide must work: apply the given 3 cm glide twice. A 3 cm slide need not work;
Border G is a counterexample. Do not infer that 6 is necessarily the shortest matching slide, since
the hypothesis only gives one matching glide.
Problem 4: Border E is a construction. The perpendicular flips force a half-turn at their
intersection. As the border already repeats, composing these flips and the period generates
further symmetries: translated copies of the perpendicular mirror line, intermediate perpendicular
mirror lines, half-turn centers, and glides formed from the middle-line flip and translations. For E,
reflections occur in y = 0 and in x = 3k, half-turn centers at (3k,0), slides by 6k, and glides along y
= 0 by nonzero 6k. The two crossing flips alone do not produce a nonzero translation; the
periodicity is a separate given feature.
Problem 5: Border R matches by a half-turn and has neither a middle-line reflection nor any
perpendicular reflection. At an upper A, either type of reflection would require one of the missing
mirror forms. The lack of those forms rules out every possible perpendicular axis, not only the axis
through the displayed center.
Problem 6: Answers are construction-dependent. A complete answer for G is: translations by 6k
cm (k ≠ 0 for a moving slide), glides along y = 0 by (6k + 3) cm, no pure reflection, and no
nonidentity rotation. Include the identity only if discussing the full group. For R: translations by 6k
cm and half-turns about (1.5 + 3k,0), with no reflections or glides. Negative displacements are
included.
Why these descriptions are complete
For these nonempty bounded-width discrete borders, the unbounded direction is the horizontal
direction. An isometry preserving the border must preserve that direction, so its linear part is one
of the four sign changes: identity, horizontal reflection, vertical reflection, or a half-turn. A nonzero
vertical translation is impossible for a bounded-width pattern. The symmetric two-row examples
force the line or centers to have y = 0. The asymmetric motif then forces the listed orientation,
and its anchor forces exactly the stated x offsets. This is an adult completeness argument;
children can explain the corresponding anchor-and-direction obstruction concretely.
Optional extension: Compare H and G. Both have matching glides, but only H has the bare
reflection. Ask which shortest-distance relationship changes and why. Seven frieze names are not
needed to settle this question.

Bellingham Math Circle / Week 35 / Adult facilitator guide
Proofs and source notes
Shortest glide theorem
The translations form P times the integers. Suppose G_a is a symmetry along y = 0. Because H
and horizontal translations commute, G_a² = T_2a, so 2a is an integer multiple of P. Composing
G_a with any matching translation changes its displacement by a multiple of P. Reduce a modulo P
into [0,P). The only possibilities are 0 and P/2. If the remainder were 0, composing with the inverse
translation would make H itself a symmetry. Thus when H fails, the remainder is P/2 and the least
absolute nonzero glide displacement is P/2. Any two glides along the same axis differ by a
matching translation, so all their displacements are (k + 1/2)P.
If H is a symmetry, composing G_a with H gives T_a; hence glide displacements are precisely
translation displacements. Conversely, every translation composed with H gives a glide when the
displacement is nonzero. Thus the shortest nonzero glide length is P in that case.
What the finite checks establish
The independent guide check represents the exact notched polygon by integer-coordinate
vertices and verifies that no nonidentity cyclic rotation or reversal of its vertices preserves all
pairwise distances. It then checks each construction by exact positions and oriented motif type in
a periodic cell, including the larger-repeat edit. This verifies these recipes and their primitive
periods. The endless symmetry statements follow from their repetition rules and the geometric
argument on page 5, not from a finite picture's endpoints.
Important teaching distinctions: a symmetry of a footprint is not the same as a symmetry of
the arrangement; a matching glide need not split into two matching component moves; a long
drawn repeat need not be primitive; and failure around one chosen center does not rule out every
half-turn.
Sources
Joseph A. Gallian, Contemporary Abstract Algebra, author-hosted Chapter 28, Frieze Groups
and Crystallographic Groups, pp. 446-449, especially pattern II, its squared-glide translation
subgroup, and pattern VII's perpendicular reflections. Author-hosted chapter. This source supplies
the symmetry-group context; the exact notched motif, constructions and shortest-period proof
here are independently developed. The full seven-type classification is background only.
Laura Givental, Maria Nemirovskaya and Ilya Zakharevich, Math Circle by the Bay, AMS/MSRI
Mathematical Circles Library 21 (2018), Preface pp. viii-ix. It describes substantial themes,
manipulatives, dialogue and varied pace. The proposed one-hour sequence, exact motif
preparation and readiness gates here are local plans, not a report of testing these tasks in that
source.
Packet basis: current Week 35 Footprint borders: K-1 v3, Problems 1-7; Grades 2-3 and 4-5 v2,
Problems 1-6. This guide uses the revised shortest-period wording, freely chosen half-turn centers,
excluded guide lines and enlarged-repeat edit convention.

Starting routes and return visits
Planning update of 4 October 2026. The timing menus are examples; a theme can continue over several meetings. Keep the full
Grades 4-5 investigations and choose by readiness.
Use and return choices
K-1 first route: Problem 1 makes one repeating border and tests matching and failing slides with a tracing
copy; Problem 2 compares two shortest slides when the first action is reliable. Keep at least three or four
visible repeats and the original fixed. Introduce the combined flip-and-slide only before Problems 3-4. On

2-3 can choose reflection or half-turn constructions and edits (P4-6). Grades 4-5 can return to forced
compositions (P3-4), or spend a visit finding all symmetries of one border (P5-6).
Entry key: K-1 Problem 1
A row of Border T copies spaced 4 cm apart matches after a 4 cm slide and fails after a 2 cm slide. Keep
the original fixed and compare several repeats; explain how the pattern continues. Children may
compare distances without measuring. The continuation key on page 4 covers Problems 2-7; the older
keys keep their original numbers.

bonus-guide.text:
Week 35 / Footprint borders / Bonus facilitator
Mathematical overview: facts, assumptions and limits
For two distinguished, fixed rows of an infinite slotted border, a matching slide must be a period of
each row. If their primitive periods are positive integers a and b slots, the shortest common matching
slide is lcm(a,b). Distinguishing rows prevents exchanging the layers. The specified asymmetric F-like
footprint has no matching nonidentity rotation; all footprints in Problems 1–2 have the same form and
orientation, so matching slides are determined by their color words. Only the endlessly repeated
pattern counts, not strip ends, construction brackets or R/B recording letters.
For recoloring a cyclic word so shift s becomes a symmetry, positions lie in cycles of i -> i+s modulo n.
Each cycle must have a single color. Its minimum edit count is its size minus its largest original color
class. Adding these independent lower bounds gives an attainable global minimum. A requested shift
may work even when a smaller shift also works; Problem 2 does not demand a primitive period equal
to s.
Two distinct forms can alternate around a necklace exactly when its number of cards is even. An odd
necklace needs at least one equal-neighbor join, and one suffices. This is a cyclic adjacency
statement, not a classification of planar necklace isometries or of seven frieze groups. Cards are
symbolic holders of two forms, and they may be turned to suit handling; their adjacency is the object
being studied.
Children discover common periods, optimal edits and a closure obstruction. Grades 2–3 have concrete
slide/edit entries; Grades 4–5 can explain orbit lower bounds and arbitrary periods. K–1 may enter
Problem 3 with adult reading and card placement. Experiments suggest rules; repeated-word/orbit
arguments and alternating closure explanations establish them.
Preparation, readiness and launch
This companion adds three investigations; it is not a prescribed extra hour. A first visit can use P1 for
15–25 minutes and start P2; a later visit can devote 15–30 minutes to each edit family or to necklace
constructions. These are unpiloted estimates. Keep the fixed KK11 / 3333 / 445 tables. Use P3 at
KK11; P1–2 at the third-grade table; offer all three and the general explanation at 445. Reading can be
adult-supported. P1 needs repeating a 2–4-card word, counting slots to 12, and comparing two fixed
rows. P2 needs keeping one original word intact, substituting colors, and counting changed positions;
fluent division or lcm notation is unnecessary. P3 needs two-way alternation and counting to eight.
Per pair: 48 same-orientation footprint cards with reusable red/blue labels, or 48 red and 48 blue
footprint cards if colors are fixed; 8 A and 8 mirror-A outline cards; two long reusable strips with 24
slots at 30 mm spacing (join paper lengths), two tracing strips, a ruler, pencil, and 8 removable join
markers. Either color supply permits any assignment to the two 24-slot strips; the supplied RBB/RBBB
start uses 14 red and 34 blue, and the RB/RBBBBBBB witness uses 15 red and 33 blue. A tracing copy
records the pattern rather than using a second card inventory. Cards can be 25 mm long with their
form and color clearly distinguished. Reuse Week 35 cards or trace the provided outline. Prepare
pieces and durable strips before class; no child cutting is needed. For the eleven-child roster budget
six pair-sized kits (two for each younger table, two at 445 so one can be demonstration/referee): 288
recolorable cards, or 288 red + 288 blue fixed-color cards; 48 A + 48 mirror-A cards, 12 slotted strips,
12 tracing strips, 6 rulers and 48 join markers. Six reusable-card kits are the lower-preparation option.
The K–1 kits may omit the strips and color labels when using P3 alone.
Build P3 necklaces directly on the table with neighboring card centers at least 30 mm apart; leave the
cards free to move rather than trying to fit them to the printed circle sites. Those 11.3 mm circles are
symbolic records: children draw a small A or mirror-A mark, or the corresponding letter, after making
a necklace. The large physical necklace and small drawing describe the same cyclic order. A partner
can place the removable join markers between actual cards. The diagrams are not placement boards
or cutting templates.
Allow two minutes of handling. Show a non-task red/blue repeat RB on one strip. Trace it, slide the
copy two slots, and keep the original fixed. Point out that the short printed word is repeated in both
directions. Before P2, use the student's non-task RBB → RRB → RRBRRB visual: one position changes
in the block and the same edit recurs in every copy. Keep an original block intact beside a repaired
Bellingham Math Circle / Week 35 / W35-BONUS-FAC-v1 / Unpiloted 1

Week 35 / Footprint borders / Bonus facilitator
block, and count only the changed positions within that block. Before P3, join the ends of a four-card
ABAB example on the table and identify the last–first neighbor pair; record the same cyclic order with
four small drawn symbols. This small closure convention does not give away the odd-case obstruction.
Physical fit, strip joins, mirror-card handling and child transfer have not been pretested. Diagrams and
code are digital checks. The material kit does not require exact pattern-block fit. One anchored adult
at each table can read, preserve state and help with tracing; adult help should not choose a repair or
route on the children's behalf.
Solutions, hints and continuations
P1 / student p. 1, two-row matching periods. Upper row RBB has primitive period 3 and lower
RBBB primitive period 4; their first shared slide is 12 slots. R marks occur every third/fourth position,
ruling out shorter primitive slides. A 6-slot pair can use RB and RBB; an 8-slot pair can use RB and
RBBBBBBB. Alternatives can have both primitive periods equal to 6 or 8. Verify the generating rule,
not only an interior window. Optional hint: keep one row's match while checking whether the other
also matches. Extension: design two rows with matching individual slides but no shared slide smaller
than their product; compare pairs whose lengths share a divisor. Ask children to justify a chosen
shortest distance rather than merely name an lcm.
P2 / student p. 2, minimum recoloring. Treat each displayed word cyclically and make the same
edits in every repeat. The cost counts positions changed within one displayed block; it does not count
the infinitely many individual footprints in the endless border. RBBBRB under shift 3 pairs positions
(1,4),(2,5),(3,6). The first two pairs disagree, giving minimum 2; all optimum words are RRBRRB,
RBBRBB, BRBBRB, BBBBBB. RBBBBRRB under shift 2 has odd/even position cycles. The odd cycle has
two R and two B, costing 2; the even cycle has three B and one R, costing 1. Minimum 3, with
RBRBRBRB or BBBBBBBB. RRBBRB under shift 2 gives two three-position cycles. Each costs 1; the
unique optimum is RBRBRB, minimum 2. Optimal repairs can create extra symmetries. Hint: follow
where one position goes under repeated requested slides; use a string ring or partner pointing before
introducing the word “cycle.” Extension: permit three colors, or prescribe two slides and compare
their merged position groups. A new number word alone is a variant of this investigation, not a fourth
counted investigation.
P3 / student p. 3, closing an alternating rule. Six and eight cards close with zero equal-neighbor
joins; five and seven cannot. Starting at A and alternating, an odd final card is A too, so the seam joins
equal forms. One equal join is attained by alternating every other join. For any binary ring, the number
of changes of form is even: returning to the start changes its form an even number of times. Thus
equal joins have the same parity as the card count. K–1 can give the last-card explanation with
objects; the parity formulation is optional upper-band continuation. Further question: allow three
forms and still require unequal neighbors; all rings of size at least three become possible. Do not
count this small changed rule as a separate delivered investigation.
Distinction, provenance and checks
Base Week 35 K–1/2–3/4–5 packets explore individual repeating borders, glides, broken matching
motions and composition/classification (see base Problems 1–6). New P1 keeps two layers
distinguished and designs common periods; P2 optimizes fixed-position recolorings rather than
moving footprints to break a motion; P3 changes the global object to a closed neighbor cycle. None
reproduces Week 1 pattern-block games, cube-stack tilings or existing back-pocket extensions.
These are original finite designs, informed by the existing Week 35 mathematical overview and the
Week 1 encore's familiar-material/new-question structure. No downloaded problem is copied. The
outline cites Math Circle by the Bay, printed pp. viii–x, for flexible depth; that is a planning reference,
not a source of these particular problems. student/verify.py checks primitive periods, exhaustive
binary minimum repairs (all possibilities), and all binary necklaces of lengths 5–8. It establishes those
finite examples; the overview explains generalization. Sources are portable; student/build.sh
OUTPUT_DIR rebuilds bonus.pdf without repository imports. All pages are unpiloted; recording use of
W35-B1, B2 or B3 with actual questions attempted remains future organizer work.
